claims.text: Adding 2–5 at.% boron to phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve their glass-forming ability.
Adding 2–5 at.% boron will enhance the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
The proposed improvement should occur when the alloys are processed by rapid solidification under well-controlled mixing conditions.
Boron contents that are too low to alter alloy structure will not provide the proposed benefit.
Excessive boron may cause phase separation.
Excessive boron may cause embrittlement or otherwise degrade mechanical properties.
Boron incorporation increases local atomic packing density.
Boron incorporation enhances short-range order and topological frustration.
Enhanced short-range order and topological frustration hinder the formation of crystalline nuclei.
Boron atoms disrupt regular atomic arrangements because of their small size and bonding characteristics.
Boron-induced structural disruption reduces atomic mobility.
Boron addition increases the critical cooling rate required for crystallization.
Boron addition raises the glass-transition temperature.
Relative to the boron-free baseline, the boron-modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation.
Relative to the boron-free baseline, the boron-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature and/or glass-transition temperature.
The magnitude and optimum concentration of the boron effect may vary among alloy systems and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that boron increases a critical cooling rate, whereas the predicted outcome states that boron lowers the critical cooling rate for glass formation. The phrase 'critical cooling rate required for crystallization' is nonstandard and is not reconciled with the lower glass-formation critical cooling rate.
